title: Server+ V5 (SK0-005) practice exam
note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from the public SK0-005 exam objectives. Not real exam questions.

q.q: A 42U rack already holds 30U of gear. How many more 2U servers can you mount, leaving no space for anything else?
o: That would leave 4U unused.
That's the free rack units, not the number of 2U servers.
Right. 42 − 30 = 12U free, and 12 ÷ 2U = 6 servers.
That divides the whole rack by 2U and ignores the 30U already used.

q.q: A server's OS has frozen and nobody is on site. You need to see its console and power cycle it from the office. What should you use?
o: The baseboard management controller (iLO, iDRAC or IPMI)
Right. Out-of-band management runs on its own chip and port, so it works even when the OS is hung.
Remote Desktop to the server's normal IP address
RDP needs a working OS, and this one is frozen.
A Wake-on-LAN magic packet sent from your desk to the server
WOL can only power on a machine that's off; it can't show a console or reset a hung OS.
SSH to the server's production network interface
SSH also depends on the hung OS.

q.q: A server has two hot-swap power supplies. How should they be cabled for the best protection?
o: Both supplies to one UPS outlet through a splitter
A single outlet and splitter is still a single point of failure.
Both supplies to the same PDU to keep cables tidy
One PDU or breaker failure would cut both supplies.
Each supply to a different PDU on a different circuit
Right. A/B feeds mean one PDU or breaker can fail without taking the server down.
One supply plugged in, the other kept as a cold spare
Then a supply failure means an outage until someone swaps it.

q.q: The server room uses hot and cold aisles. Half the rack spaces in one rack are empty, and the servers above them run hot. What fixes this most directly?
o: Remove the rack's side panels to let more air in
Open sides mix hot and cold air and break the aisle design.
Move the hottest servers to the top of the rack
Heat rises; the top of a rack is usually the warmest spot.
Install blanking panels in the empty rack spaces
Right. Blanking panels stop hot exhaust air from looping back to the server intakes.
Turn every server around so it faces the hot aisle
Intakes must face the cold aisle; reversing them makes it worse.

q.q: You're loading a new, empty rack with two heavy storage arrays, four 1U servers and a UPS. Where should the heaviest gear go?
o: At the top so cables reach the ceiling tray
Heavy gear up high makes the rack top-heavy and unsafe.
At the bottom of the rack
Right. Heavy gear low keeps the rack's center of gravity low so it won't tip.
In the middle at eye level for easy service
Convenience doesn't outweigh tipping risk for the heaviest units.
Spread evenly so each rack unit holds equal weight
Gear doesn't divide that way; you put the heaviest items lowest.

q.q: A UPS is rated 1500 VA / 900 W. The servers plugged into it draw a total of 1,000 W at 1,150 VA. What happens?
o: It's fine because UPS units can run at 150% all day
Overload capacity lasts seconds, not continuously.
The UPS is overloaded because the watt limit is exceeded
Right. Both ratings must be met; 1,000 W is above the 900 W limit even though VA is under 1500.
It's fine because 1,150 VA is under the 1500 VA rating
VA is only half the check; watts are over the limit.
It's overloaded because VA must stay under the watt rating
VA is normally higher than watts; that's not the rule.

q.q: A server on sliding rails must be pulled out for service without unplugging anything. What should you install?
o: Zip ties fastening each cable to the rack's rear rails
That locks the cables in place so the server can't move.
A cable management arm with labeled service loops
Right. The arm folds out with the server and the slack keeps cables connected.
Shorter patch cables pulled tight to the rack frame
Tight cables would unplug or break when the server slides out.
A second set of rails mounted behind the first set
Extra rails don't manage cables.

q.q: What does a blade enclosure give the blade servers inside it?
o: Wireless links so blades need no network cables
Blades connect through the chassis backplane and switch modules.
A dedicated hypervisor that each blade must run
The chassis doesn't choose an OS or hypervisor.
Shared power, cooling, networking and management
Right. Blades are small boards that rely on the chassis for those shared services.
Separate fans and power supplies inside each blade
That's a rack server; blades share the chassis supplies and fans.

q.q: You build a RAID 5 array from four 2 TB drives. How much usable space do you get?
o: 8 TB
That's raw space with no parity.
6 TB
Right. RAID 5 gives up one drive's worth of space for parity: (4 − 1) × 2 TB.
2 TB
That's a single drive; RAID 5 is not a four-way mirror.
4 TB
That's RAID 10 or RAID 6 with four drives.

q.q: A database server does many small random writes and must survive a drive failure. Which RAID level gives the best write performance?
o: RAID 5
Every write also updates parity, the RAID 5 write penalty.
RAID 6
Double parity makes the write penalty even bigger.
RAID 0
Fast, but one failed drive loses all the data.
RAID 10
Right. Striped mirrors have no parity to calculate, so writes are fast and still redundant.

q.q: A file archive uses eight 16 TB drives. A rebuild takes more than a day, and a second drive could fail during it. Which RAID level fits best?
o: RAID 6
Right. Dual parity survives two drive failures, which covers a second failure during a long rebuild.
RAID 0
No redundancy at all.
RAID 1
A two-drive mirror can't use eight drives as one volume.
RAID 5
It survives only one failure, so a second failure mid-rebuild loses the array.

q.q: The office wants shared storage for virtual machines but has no Fibre Channel switches, only 10 Gb Ethernet. What should you use?
o: Fibre Channel over a new fabric
That needs FC switches and HBAs, which they don't have.
USB external drives on each host
Not shared storage, and far too slow.
iSCSI
Right. iSCSI carries block storage (SCSI) over normal IP networks.
A NAS share over SMB for the VMs
SMB is file-level; the question asks for a block SAN design.

q.q: Users need shared department folders they open as network drives using SMB. Which storage fits?
o: DAS
Direct-attached storage connects to one server, not to the network.
JBOD
Just a bunch of disks; it isn't a network file service.
NAS
Right. A NAS serves files at the file level over SMB or NFS.
SAN LUN
A SAN gives block storage to servers, not folders to users.

q.q: A RAID controller uses write-back cache. Why does it need a battery or flash backup module?
o: To keep cached writes safe if power is lost
Right. Write-back reports writes as done before they reach disk, so cache must survive a power loss.
To power the drives during a hot swap
Drives get power from the backplane, not the cache module.
To speed up reads by spinning drives faster
The module protects cache; it doesn't change drive speed.
To store the RAID level settings for the BIOS
Array settings live in the controller and on the drives.

q.q: A RAID 5 array has a drive configured as a global hot spare. What happens when an array drive fails?
o: The array goes offline until the failed drive is replaced
RAID 5 keeps running degraded, and the spare rebuilds it.
The spare joins the array and the rebuild starts on its own
Right. That's what a hot spare is for: no one has to swap a drive before the rebuild starts.
The spare turns RAID 5 into RAID 6 automatically
A spare restores redundancy; it doesn't change the RAID level.
The spare stays idle until a tech assigns it to the array
That's a cold spare.

q.q: A transaction log volume needs the lowest possible latency. Which drive type fits best?
o: 15K RPM SAS HDD
Spinning disks have seek time; even fast ones are slower than flash.
NVMe SSD
Right. NVMe talks over PCIe lanes and skips the SATA/SAS controller, so it has the lowest latency.
SATA SSD
Fast, but the SATA interface adds latency and caps throughput.
7.2K RPM SATA HDD
The slowest option in this list.

q.q: You have a SAS RAID controller and a backplane. Which statement about drives is true?
o: SAS and SATA drives can never share the same controller
Many SAS controllers accept both.
Any drive works on any controller if the RAID is rebuilt
Interface compatibility doesn't change with a rebuild.
SATA drives work on a SAS controller, but not the other way around
Right. SAS controllers are backward compatible with SATA drives; it doesn't work the other way.
SAS drives work on a SATA controller, but SATA drives won't work on a SAS one
That's backward.

q.q: A RAID 5 array is degraded. Two drives look identical. How do you make sure you pull the failed one?
o: Power off the server and test each drive in a separate PC first
That causes an outage and isn't needed.
Use the controller's locate function or the drive's fault LED
Right. Pulling a healthy drive from a degraded RAID 5 destroys the array.
Pull the drive in the lowest-numbered bay first
Bay order doesn't tell you which one failed.
Pull the drive that feels the warmest to the touch
Heat doesn't show which drive failed.

q.q: A cluster node needs a BIOS/UEFI update. What should you do before applying it?
o: Apply it to every node at once to keep versions matched
Updating all nodes together risks the whole cluster.
Read the release notes for prerequisites and known issues
Right. Some updates need a certain BMC or firmware version first, or have known bugs.
Reset the BIOS to factory defaults to clear old settings
That could wipe needed settings like boot order or RAID mode.
Disable the BMC so the update can't be interrupted
You often need the BMC to watch or recover the update.

q.q: You're replacing a DIMM in a server. Which precaution protects the parts?
o: Wear rubber gloves so static can't build up
Gloves don't drain static; a grounded strap does.
Wear an antistatic wrist strap clipped to the chassis
Right. It keeps you at the same potential as the chassis so static doesn't zap the parts.
Leave the server plugged in so it stays grounded
Work inside a powered server is a shock and damage risk; unplug it.
Touch the DIMM's gold contacts to discharge them
Touching contacts adds oil and static; hold modules by the edges.

q.q: Where can you see a server's hardware event history, such as fan or power faults, even when no OS is installed?
o: The Windows Application event log
That needs Windows running and logs apps, not hardware.
The switch port's interface counters
That only shows network errors for that port.
The /var/log/messages file on the server
That's an OS log, and there's no OS here.
The BMC's System Event Log (SEL)
Right. The SEL is kept by the management controller, independent of the OS.

q.q: After you add four DIMMs, the server runs but memory is slower than expected. The DIMMs work. What's the most likely cause?
o: RAM always runs slower until the server is burned in
There's no burn-in period for memory speed.
The RAID controller cache is using the new DIMMs
The RAID cache is separate memory on the controller.
They're in the wrong slots for the board's channel layout
Right. Boards need DIMMs in matching channels to run in multichannel mode.
The new DIMMs need an updated OS memory driver before they run at full speed
RAM doesn't use an OS driver for speed.

q.q: Monitoring shows SMART predictive-failure alerts on one drive in a RAID 6 array. The drive still works. What should you do?
o: Turn off SMART monitoring to stop the alerts
That hides the warning instead of fixing the problem.
Run a full disk defragmentation on the volume
Defragmenting adds wear and doesn't fix a failing drive.
Leave it until the drive actually fails, since RAID 6 can lose two drives
RAID 6 can lose two drives, but waiting reduces your margin.
Replace it during a planned window before it fails
Right. Predictive failure means it's likely to die soon; swap it while the array is healthy.

q.q: A new server boots from a single 4 TB volume. Which setup lets the OS use the whole disk as a boot drive?
o: UEFI firmware with a GPT partition table
Right. MBR tops out at 2 TB; GPT with UEFI boot handles much larger disks.
MBR with four primary partitions of 1 TB each
MBR still can't boot or address past 2 TB.
Legacy BIOS with an MBR partition table
MBR can't address more than 2 TB.
Legacy BIOS with an extended MBR partition
Extended partitions don't lift the 2 TB limit.

q.q: You must install the same OS on 40 new servers that have no optical drives. What's the most efficient method?
o: Burn 40 DVDs and attach USB DVD drives
Slow and manual for 40 servers.
Network (PXE) boot into an image deployment server
Right. PXE boots from the network so one image can go to many servers at once.
Install each server by hand from a USB stick
Works, but it's the slowest option at this scale.
Clone one server's drive by moving it to each server
Error prone and needs physical swaps.

q.q: You want installs to run with no one answering prompts. What do you provide to the installer?
o: A golden performance baseline report exported from an existing server
A baseline records performance; it doesn't drive an install.
An answer file such as unattend.xml or a kickstart file
Right. Answer files feed the installer every setting so it runs unattended.
The license key typed into the BIOS settings
The BIOS doesn't pass installer settings.
A runbook a tech follows step by step
That's still a person answering prompts.

q.q: Which filesystem do VMware ESXi hosts use for their datastores on block storage?
o: VMFS
Right. VMFS is VMware's clustered filesystem that lets several hosts share a datastore.
FAT32
FAT32 can't hold files over 4 GB, and ESXi doesn't use it for datastores.
ReFS
ReFS is Microsoft's resilient filesystem.
XFS
XFS is a Linux filesystem.

q.q: A Windows server only runs DNS and DHCP and will be managed remotely. Which install option reduces patching and attack surface?
o: Desktop Experience with the firewall turned off
Turning off the firewall increases risk.
Desktop Experience with every role added
More components mean more patches and more risk.
A client OS like Windows 11 Enterprise
Client editions aren't built to host server roles.
Server Core with no desktop experience
Right. No GUI means fewer components to patch or attack.

q.q: The internal DNS server got its address from DHCP and came back with a new IP after a reboot. Clients can't resolve names. What's the best long-term fix?
o: Shorten the DHCP lease to one hour
Shorter leases make address changes more likely.
Restart the DHCP server every night
That doesn't stop the address from changing.
Give it a static IP outside the DHCP scope
Right. Infrastructure servers need addresses that never change.
Add the new IP to every client's hosts file
Hosts files don't scale and break again on the next change.

q.q: A server connects to two different switches that don't support link aggregation. You need failover if one switch dies. Which NIC team mode fits?
o: Switch-independent active/standby
Right. It works without switch support and fails over to the standby NIC.
LACP (802.3ad) active/active
LACP needs both links on switches configured for aggregation.
A single NIC with a second IP address
One NIC is still a single point of failure.
Static link aggregation across both switches
Static aggregation also needs switch configuration.

q.q: A virtualization host runs VMs on VLAN 10, 20 and 30 over one physical NIC. How must the switch port be set?
o: As an access port in VLAN 10
An access port carries one untagged VLAN.
As an access port in VLAN 1
VLAN 1 is just the default; the VMs need 10, 20 and 30.
As an access port with spanning tree turned off for speed
STP settings don't decide which VLANs pass.
As an 802.1Q trunk carrying VLANs 10, 20 and 30
Right. A trunk carries tagged traffic for several VLANs on one link.

q.q: Users should reach a new intranet server by name. The name must resolve to its IPv4 address. Which DNS record do you create?
o: An AAAA record
AAAA is for IPv6 addresses.
A PTR record
PTR maps an IP back to a name (reverse lookup).
An A record
Right. A records map a hostname to an IPv4 address.
An MX record
MX names a domain's mail servers.

q.q: A server is 10.10.20.50/26. Which default gateway is valid for it?
o: That's in the next /26 (.64–.127).
That's the subnet's broadcast address.
That's a different network.
Right. A /26 holds 64 addresses; .50 sits in .0–.63, so .1 is in the same subnet.

q.q: Domain logons fail with Kerberos errors, and the server's clock is 12 minutes off. What should every server be set up to use?
o: A reliable NTP time source
Right. Kerberos rejects tickets when clocks differ too much (5 minutes by default).
A longer DHCP lease time
DHCP leases don't set the clock.
A larger DNS cache size
DNS caching has nothing to do with clock skew.
A static ARP entry for the DC
ARP maps IPs to MACs, not time.

q.q: Before a major application upgrade, you record CPU, memory, disk and network use during a normal week. Why?
o: To create a baseline to compare against after the upgrade
Right. A baseline shows what normal looked like, so you can spot changes.
To set the length of the DHCP leases
Lease time isn't based on server performance.
To choose a RAID level for the new data volume
RAID is chosen from redundancy and I/O needs, not a usage log.
To meet the software vendor's license audit requirements for upgrades
License audits count installs, not performance.

q.q: You're moving a file share to a new server and must keep NTFS permissions and timestamps. What should you use?
o: A copy tool that keeps ACLs, such as robocopy /COPYALL
Right. Plain copies take the new folder's permissions and lose the originals.
Drag and drop in File Explorer
A normal copy inherits the destination's permissions.
Zip the share, then unzip it on the new server
Zip files don't keep NTFS permissions.
Email the files to users to save again
Slow, insecure and loses permissions.

q.q: Which is the safest way to apply monthly OS patches to production servers?
o: Test in staging, then patch in a maintenance window with a rollback plan
Right. Testing finds problems first; the window and rollback limit the impact.
Skip patches unless a server has a problem
Unpatched servers stay open to known attacks.
Patch every production server the same day the vendor releases the patches
Untested patches can break production all at once.
Let each user decide when their server reboots
Uncontrolled reboots cause outages and missed patches.

q.q: A server shows 15% CPU, 40% memory and 60 ms disk latency with a long disk queue all day. Users say it's slow. Where's the bottleneck?
o: CPU
15% CPU is low.
Network
Nothing here points to the network.
Memory
40% use leaves plenty free.
Storage I/O
Right. High latency and a long queue mean requests are waiting on the disks.

q.q: In a two-node cluster, one node runs the service while the other waits idle and takes over only when the first fails. What is this?
o: Round robin load balancing
That spreads requests across working nodes.
Active-active
Both nodes would serve traffic at the same time.
A cold site arrangement
A cold site is a disaster recovery location.
Active-passive
Right. One node serves; the passive node takes over on failure.

q.q: A two-node cluster loses its heartbeat link. Both nodes think the other died and both try to own the shared disk. What prevents this?
o: A longer heartbeat timeout on both nodes
That delays the problem; it doesn't settle which node wins.
A quorum witness that breaks the tie
Right. The witness gives a third vote so only one side keeps running (no split brain).
Turning off failover until the link is back
That gives up high availability.
Running both nodes in active-active mode
Both owning the same disk is the split-brain problem.

q.q: A failed cluster node is repaired, and services move back to it from the other node. What is this called?
o: Fault tolerance
Fault tolerance is about not stopping at all.
Failover
Failover moves services away from a failed node.
Heartbeat
Heartbeat is the health check between nodes.
Failback
Right. Failback returns services to the original node after it's healthy.

q.q: A web farm's sessions vary from seconds to an hour. Which load balancing method spreads the work most evenly?
o: Round robin
It ignores how busy each server is, so long sessions pile up.
Source IP hash
It keeps a client on one server; it doesn't balance load.
Least connections
Right. New requests go to the server with the fewest active sessions.
Active-passive
Only one server would take traffic.

q.q: A server connects to the SAN through two HBAs on two separate fabrics. What lets it use both paths and survive losing one?
o: NIC teaming
Teaming is for Ethernet NICs, not SAN HBAs.
A larger LUN
Size doesn't add a path.
Multipath I/O (MPIO)
Right. MPIO treats both paths as one device and fails over between them.
RAID 1 on the HBAs
RAID protects drives, not paths.

q.q: Which hypervisor type runs directly on the hardware and is used for production servers?
o: A container runtime
Containers share a host OS kernel; they aren't hypervisors.
Type 2 (hosted)
Type 2 runs as an app on a desktop OS, like VirtualBox.
A guest operating system
Guests run inside VMs on a hypervisor.
Type 1 (bare metal)
Right. Type 1 hypervisors like ESXi and Hyper-V run on the hardware with no host OS underneath.

q.q: A host has 64 GB of RAM. Its VMs are assigned a total of 96 GB. What's the risk?
o: If all VMs use their full memory, the host swaps and slows down
Right. That's memory overcommitment, which only works while VMs don't all need their full memory.
The VMs get 64 GB each because RAM is shared
VMs can't use more than the host physically has.
The hypervisor refuses to start any VM until the total fits in 64 GB
Most hypervisors allow overcommitment.
There's no risk because unused RAM is deleted
Unused RAM isn't deleted; the risk comes when it's needed.

q.q: Three test VMs must talk to each other but not to the host or the physical network. Which Hyper-V virtual switch type fits?
o: Default trunk
Not a Hyper-V switch type.
Internal
Internal also connects the host.
Private
Right. A private switch connects VMs only to each other.
External
External connects VMs to the physical network.

q.q: A unit keeps sensitive records in its own data center but runs its public website in a public cloud, with the two linked. Which cloud model is this?
o: Community cloud
A community cloud is shared by organizations with common needs.
Hybrid cloud
Right. Hybrid combines on-premises or private cloud with public cloud.
Public cloud
Some of the workload stays on premises.
Private cloud
Private cloud alone doesn't include public cloud.

q.q: What's the relationship between a host and a guest in virtualization?
o: The guest is the management workstation that connects to and controls the host
That's a management workstation, not a guest.
The host runs the hypervisor; the guest is a VM on top of it
Right. The host provides the hardware resources the guests use.
Hosts and guests are two names for one VM
They're different roles.
The guest runs the hypervisor; the host is the VM
That's backward.

q.q: Which file extension goes with a PowerShell script?
o: .ps1
Right. PowerShell scripts use .ps1.
.vbs
VBScript.
.sh
Bash shell scripts.
.bat
Batch files run in cmd.exe.

q.q:
What does this bash script do?

for s in web1 web2 web3; do
  ssh $s "systemctl is-active nginx" || echo "$s down"
done
o: Restarts nginx on web1, web2 and web3 one at a time and logs any that fail
is-active only checks status; it doesn't restart.
Checks nginx on three servers and prints the names where it isn't running
Right. || runs the echo only when the check fails.
Installs nginx on any server that lacks it
Nothing here installs software.
Prints down for every server no matter what
The echo runs only after a failed check.

q.q: In PowerShell, which condition is true when $freeGB is less than 10?
o: if ($freeGB < 10)
< is a redirection operator in PowerShell, not a comparison.
if ($freeGB -lt 10)
Right. PowerShell uses -lt for less than.
if ($freeGB -gt 10)
-gt is greater than.
if ($freeGB -eq 10)
-eq is equal to.

q.q: You need to restart the same service on 25 servers listed in a text file. Which script element does the repeating?
o: A constant
A constant stores a value that doesn't change.
A comment
Comments are notes; they don't run.
A comparison
A comparison checks a condition; it doesn't repeat.
A loop
Right. A loop runs the same steps for each item in the list.

q.q: Which document shows exactly which rack units each server, switch and PDU occupies?
o: A rack elevation diagram
Right. It draws each device's position in the rack.
A performance baseline
A baseline records normal performance.
A logical network diagram
That shows IPs, subnets and flows, not rack positions.
A service level agreement
An SLA sets performance and uptime terms.

q.q: A tech needs step-by-step instructions to restore the mail server after a failure. Which document should exist?
o: A runbook
Right. Runbooks give repeatable steps for a specific task.
A warranty certificate
That proves coverage, not how to recover.
A purchase order
That's for buying equipment.
An asset tag list
Tags identify hardware; they don't explain recovery.

q.q: A critical server needs vendor parts on site within hours, any time of day. Which support contract fits?
o: Standard warranty with mail-in repair
Mail-in can take weeks.
Self-maintenance with no vendor contract
You'd need your own spares and parts.
Next-business-day parts replacement
A failure Friday night could wait until Monday.
24x7 coverage with a 4-hour response
Right. Fast, round-the-clock response matches a critical system.

q.q: Which stage of the asset life cycle includes data sanitization and recycling?
o: Procurement
That's buying the asset.
Disposal
Right. End of life covers wiping, destroying and recycling.
Deployment
That's putting it into service.
Maintenance
That's patching, fixing and upgrading in service.

q.q: A product is licensed per physical core, sold in 2-core packs. The host has 2 CPUs with 12 cores each. How many packs do you need?
o: That counts sockets.
Right. 2 × 12 = 24 cores, and 24 ÷ 2 = 12 packs.
That only covers one CPU.
That counts cores, not 2-core packs.

q.q: Forty shift workers share six kiosk PCs to reach a server app. Which client license model costs the least?
o: Per device
Right. Six devices need six licenses instead of forty user licenses.
Per core
That licenses the server, not client access.
Site license
A site license is usually priced for a whole location and costs more here.
Per user
That needs forty licenses.

q.q: What happens when a subscription license isn't renewed?
o: You keep the current version forever with no updates
That describes a perpetual license.
It turns into an open-source license
Licenses don't convert like that.
Nothing changes until the next audit
Use without a valid license breaks the terms right away.
Your right to use the software or get updates ends
Right. Subscriptions grant use for a set term only.

q.q: Which is true about open-source software on a production server?
o: It always comes with a paid vendor support contract you must renew yearly
Support is optional and often separate.
It can't be used by government agencies
Government agencies use open source widely.
Open-source software has no license at all
It has a license; it's just an open one.
There's usually no license fee, but the license terms still apply
Right. Licenses like GPL set rules for sharing changes, even when the software is free.

q.q: A server's drives might be stolen during shipping to a new site. Which control keeps the data unreadable?
o: Full-disk encryption at rest
Right. Without the key, a stolen encrypted drive is unreadable.
A strong local administrator password
Someone can read the drive in another machine and skip the OS login.
TLS on the server's web service
TLS protects data moving over the network, not sitting on disk.
A locking bezel on the drive bays
A bezel slows removal; it doesn't protect a drive already taken.

q.q: Which choice protects files while they move between two servers over the network?
o: FTP on a nonstandard port
A different port doesn't add encryption.
SFTP instead of FTP
Right. SFTP encrypts the session; FTP sends files and passwords in clear text.
Full-disk encryption on both servers
That protects data at rest, not in transit.
Telnet with a long password
Telnet is unencrypted too.

q.q: Someone with physical access could boot a server from a USB stick and bypass its OS controls. Which setting helps stop this?
o: A DHCP reservation for the server's NIC
IP settings don't control the boot device.
A larger swap file on the system disk
Swap size has nothing to do with boot control.
A longer screen saver timeout on the console
That doesn't control what the server boots from.
A UEFI/BIOS admin password and a locked boot order
Right. Locking firmware settings stops someone from changing the boot device.

q.q: A regulation says audit logs must be kept for three years, then destroyed. Which policy covers this?
o: Change management
That controls how changes are approved.
Data retention
Right. Retention policies set how long data is kept and when it's disposed of.
Acceptable use
That covers how users may use systems.
Password complexity
That sets password rules.

q.q: Visitors keep following staff through the server room door. Which control stops one badge letting two people in?
o: An access control vestibule (mantrap)
Right. Two interlocked doors let only one person through per badge.
A security camera aimed at the door
Cameras record tailgating but don't stop it.
A longer door-close delay
A slower door makes tailgating easier.
A sign that says authorized personnel only
A sign deters but doesn't prevent.

q.q: Contractors work in the server room under escort. What stops someone from quickly pulling hot-swap drives from a server?
o: Full-disk encryption on every drive
Encryption protects data on a stolen drive but doesn't stop the theft.
A badge reader on the building's main entrance
That's an outer layer; the contractors are already inside.
Locking front bezels and locked rack doors
Right. A physical lock at the rack stops removal even inside the room.
Antivirus on every server
Antivirus doesn't stop physical removal.

q.q: Which fire suppression fits a server room best?
o: A dry chemical powder system
Powder is corrosive and leaves residue in the equipment.
Standard wet-pipe sprinklers above the racks
Water damages running equipment.
Handheld water extinguishers only
Water on live electrical gear is dangerous.
A clean agent system that leaves no residue
Right. Clean agents put out fires without water damage to electronics.

q.q: A backup application needs a Windows account to run its service. Which choice follows least privilege?
o: A shared account whose password everyone knows
Shared accounts can't be audited and are easy to misuse.
A senior technician's personal domain user account with admin rights
The service breaks when that person leaves, and their actions blur together.
The built-in domain Administrator account
Far more power than a backup service needs.
A dedicated service account with only the rights it needs
Right. A separate, limited account limits damage if it's compromised.

q.q: Twelve analysts need read access to the same five server shares. What's the easiest access model to manage?
o: Have the analysts share one account
No accountability for who did what.
Grant each analyst rights on each share
Sixty separate permissions are hard to keep correct.
Put them in a group and grant the group access
Right. Role-based access through groups is easy to audit and change.
Give everyone full control and trust them
That breaks least privilege.

q.q: Admins log on to servers with a password plus a code from a smart card or authenticator. What does this add?
o: Role-based access control
RBAC decides permissions, not how you prove identity.
Multifactor authentication
Right. It combines something you know with something you have.
Single sign-on
SSO reduces logins; it doesn't add a factor by itself.
Account lockout
Lockout limits guessing; it isn't a second factor.

q.q: After an outage, nobody can tell which admin changed a firewall rule on a server. What should have been in place?
o: Named admin accounts with auditing turned on
Right. Personal accounts plus audit logs show who did what and when.
A shorter password expiration period
That doesn't record actions.
A single shared admin account for the team
Shared accounts are why nobody can tell.
A larger security log with no account changes
Logs only help if each admin has their own account.

q.q: An admin with broad access copied a large set of personnel files to a USB drive before leaving. Which controls best reduce this risk?
o: More bandwidth to the file server
Speed doesn't stop data loss.
Faster backups, more RAID drives and a bigger backup library
Those protect availability, not leaks.
A stronger perimeter firewall
The threat was already inside the network.
Least privilege, DLP and auditing of file access
Right. Limiting access, blocking or flagging transfers and logging use all target insider risk.

q.q: A scan finds a share with personal records open to Everyone with Full Control. What's the risk?
o: Running out of licenses for the share
Shares don't use licenses that way.
A failed RAID rebuild on the volume
RAID has nothing to do with permissions.
Unwanted access and data exposure
Right. Anyone on the network can read, change or delete the records.
Slower file transfers for users
Permissions don't affect speed.

q.q: Legal says records about an ongoing investigation must not be deleted, even if the retention period ends. What is this?
o: A data retention policy
Retention sets normal keep-and-delete times; the hold overrides it.
A legal hold
Right. A legal hold overrides normal deletion until it's lifted.
A data loss prevention rule
DLP stops data leaving; it doesn't freeze deletion.
A data classification label
Classification marks sensitivity, not deletion holds.

q.q: A new Linux server is built for a single web app. What's the first hardening step after patching?
o: Open all ports so monitoring tools can connect
That widens the attack surface.
Disable or remove services and accounts the app doesn't need
Right. Every unused service or account is something to attack.
Turn off logging to save disk space
Logs are needed to spot and investigate attacks.
Install a full desktop environment so admins can manage it more easily
More software means more to patch and attack.

q.q: A security scan flags every server's iLO and iDRAC as using the factory password. What should you do?
o: Set unique strong passwords and limit BMC access to a management network
Right. Default BMC credentials give full control of the hardware.
Change only the OS administrator passwords
BMC credentials are separate from the OS.
Leave them as they are, since BMCs aren't reachable from outside the base network
Insiders and malware inside can still reach them.
Unplug the BMC ports permanently
You'd lose out-of-band management.

q.q: Your command must configure servers to a published DoD security baseline. What should you apply?
o: The matching DISA STIG
Right. STIGs are DoD's secure configuration guides.
A data retention schedule
That's about keeping records.
A RAID 6 storage policy
That's about storage, not configuration hardening.
The vendor's default install settings
Defaults favor ease of use, not security.

q.q: A Windows file server still accepts SMBv1. What should you do?
o: Turn on SMBv1 encryption
SMBv1 doesn't support encryption.
Disable SMBv1 after confirming nothing needs it
Right. SMBv1 is old and has had serious exploits used by worms.
Rename the SMBv1 service
Renaming doesn't fix the protocol.
Block SMB with the host firewall entirely
That breaks file sharing for everyone.

q.q: A server is being retired. Which order is right?
o: Wipe the drives, migrate the data, update the inventory, then remove it from DNS and monitoring
You can't migrate data after wiping it.
Update inventory, unplug it, migrate data later from the drives
The data should move before shutdown.
Remove from DNS, recycle it, then wipe the drives
Drives must be wiped before they leave your control.
Migrate data, remove it from DNS and monitoring, wipe the drives, update the inventory
Right. Move the data first, then clean up references, sanitize and document.

q.q: Retired servers have SSDs with sensitive data. Why isn't a single overwrite pass enough?
o: SSDs can't be written to once they're removed
They can still be written to in another system.
SSD data fades by itself after a few days
Flash keeps data much longer than that.
Wear leveling can leave old data in blocks the overwrite never reaches
Right. Use crypto erase, the drive's secure erase or physical destruction.
Overwriting every block of an SSD always damages the flash chips right away
One pass doesn't destroy the drive.

q.q: A contractor shreds retired drives. What should you get from them?
o: A new warranty for the destroyed drives
Destroyed drives have no warranty.
The shredded pieces mailed back to you
That isn't how destruction is documented.
A certificate of destruction listing each serial number
Right. It proves which drives were destroyed and when.
A full copy of the data on each drive, made right before shredding
That defeats the purpose.

q.q: Full backups run on Sunday and differentials every other night. The server fails Thursday morning. What do you restore?
o: Sunday's full only
That loses Monday through Wednesday.
Sunday's full and Wednesday's differential
Right. Each differential has everything since the last full, so you need only the latest one.
Wednesday's differential alone
A differential needs the full under it.
Sunday's full and every differential since
You only need the newest differential.

q.q: Full backups run on Sunday and incrementals every other night. The server fails Thursday morning. What do you restore?
o: Sunday's full only
That loses three days of changes.
Wednesday's incremental alone
An incremental needs the full and every incremental before it.
Sunday's full plus Wednesday's incremental, since it's the newest one
That skips Monday's and Tuesday's changes.
Sunday's full and the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday incrementals
Right. Each incremental has only changes since the last backup, so you need them all in order.

q.q: Which practice best proves your backups will work in a real outage?
o: Restoring from them on a regular schedule
Right. A backup you've never restored from is a guess.
Taking more snapshots on the production array
Snapshots live on the same storage and aren't separate backups.
Keeping backups on the same array as the data
One failure would take both.
Checking that the backup job says Completed
Jobs can finish with bad or missing data.

q.q: Which setup follows the 3-2-1 backup rule?
o: Three copies of the data, on two types of media, with one off site
Right. 3-2-1 survives a media failure and a site loss.
One full backup a week kept for three weeks
That's a schedule, not 3-2-1.
Three backups on one NAS, two of them encrypted, one tested
Everything on one NAS fails together.
Two copies on site and one VM snapshot
Snapshots on the same host don't count as off site.

q.q: The commander says the unit can lose at most 4 hours of data in a disaster. Which value is that?
o: Mean time between failures (MTBF)
MTBF measures how reliable a part is.
Recovery point objective (RPO)
Right. RPO is how much data loss, measured in time, is acceptable.
Recovery time objective (RTO)
RTO is how long you can be down.
Mean time to repair (MTTR)
MTTR is average fix time.

q.q: A DR site has power, network and racks, plus servers with data restored from backups every few days. It needs a day or two to take over. What type is it?
o: Cold site
A cold site has space and power but no ready servers or data.
Warm site
Right. Some gear and data are ready, but it needs work before it can run.
Hot site
A hot site runs current data and takes over in minutes.
Mobile site
A mobile site is a trailer or container that moves.

q.q: Leaders walk through a hurricane scenario around a table to check that everyone knows their DR role. What kind of test is this?
o: Tabletop exercise
Right. It's a discussion-based walkthrough with no systems touched.
Full failover test
That actually moves production to the DR site.
Parallel test
That runs systems at the DR site alongside production.
Penetration test
That tests security, not DR roles.

q.q: Two data centers 1,500 miles apart must replicate a database. Which replication type fits that distance?
o: Asynchronous replication
Right. Async doesn't wait for the far site, so latency doesn't slow every write.
RAID 1 across both sites
RAID mirrors drives in one system, not across sites.
Synchronous replication
Each write would wait for the far site, slowing every write.
Daily tape shipments only
That's backup, not replication.

q.q: Users report that a file server is slow. Following CompTIA's method, what do you do first?
o: Replace the RAID controller
That's a fix without a theory.
Document the fix in the ticket
Documenting comes last.
Reboot the server to clear any hung processes, then see if users still complain
That's acting before you know the cause, and can destroy evidence.
Identify the problem: question users, check recent changes and logs
Right. You need to know the symptoms and what changed before forming a theory.

q.q: While identifying a problem, you plan to change a server's configuration to test a theory. What should you do if possible before making changes?
o: Back up the server or its configuration
Right. Server+ includes backups before changes so you can undo them.
Escalate to the vendor first
Escalate when needed, not before every change.
Tell users the server is retired
There's no reason to retire it.
Close the ticket as resolved
Nothing's fixed yet.

q.q: Your theory that a bad NIC caused an outage is wrong; a new NIC didn't help. What's the next step?
o: Implement the solution anyway
The theory wasn't confirmed.
Document the NIC as the cause
That records the wrong cause.
Form a new theory or escalate
Right. If the test fails, go back and form another theory, or escalate.
Verify full system functionality
There's no fix to verify yet.

q.q: You confirmed a full disk caused a crash and freed space. What comes right after you implement the fix?
o: Identify the problem again
The problem has been found and fixed.
Establish a theory of probable cause
You did that already.
Verify full system functionality and add preventive measures
Right. Check that everything works and stop it from happening again, like adding disk alerts.
Close the ticket, since freeing space removed the cause of the crash
Verify first.

q.q: What's the final step of the troubleshooting method?
o: Test the theory to determine the cause
That's an earlier step.
Establish a plan of action
That comes before the fix.
Document findings, actions and outcomes
Right. Documentation helps the next tech and builds a knowledge base.
Question the users
That's part of the first step.

q.q: A server shuts itself off under heavy load. The BMC log shows thermal events, and one rack has open spaces with no panels. What's the most likely cause?
o: Poor airflow causing overheating
Right. Hot air recirculating through open spaces raises intake temperature until the server shuts down to protect itself.
An operating system license that expired last week
Licensing doesn't shut down hardware.
A bad network cable
Cabling doesn't cause thermal events.
A failed CMOS battery
That causes lost time and settings, not thermal shutdowns.

q.q: Every time a server loses power, its date resets to the year 2000 and its BIOS settings go back to defaults. What should you replace?
o: The CMOS battery
Right. The battery keeps the clock and settings while AC power is off.
The system board's DIMMs
Memory loses everything without power; it doesn't hold BIOS settings.
The RAID controller battery
That protects write cache, not the system clock.
The power supply
PSUs don't hold settings when unplugged.

q.q: The BMC reports a growing number of correctable ECC errors on DIMM B3. The server hasn't crashed. What should you do?
o: Disable ECC to stop the alerts
That removes protection and hides the warning.
Schedule replacement of DIMM B3
Right. Rising correctable errors often come before uncorrectable errors and crashes.
Replace every DIMM in the server
Only one module is reporting errors.
Ignore it because ECC corrected the errors
ECC hides the errors, but the module is failing.

q.q: After adding RAM, a server beeps during POST and won't boot. What should you check first?
o: Replace the hard drives
Drives aren't part of the memory beep test.
Reinstall the operating system from the original installation media
The server isn't getting past POST to load the OS.
Update the NIC firmware
NIC firmware doesn't stop POST.
That the new DIMMs are seated, supported and in the right slots
Right. New memory is the change, so it's the first suspect.

q.q: A server with two power supplies shows an amber light on PSU 2 but keeps running. What does this mean?
o: The server will shut down in 10 minutes
Redundant supplies keep it running.
Both supplies are fine; an amber light just means the second supply is on standby
Amber normally signals a fault.
PSU 2 or its power feed failed, and the server has lost power redundancy
Right. It runs on PSU 1, but another failure would take it down.
The CPU is overheating
PSU LEDs show power status, not CPU temperature.

q.q: A server was moved to a new rack and won't power on. No lights at all. What should you check first?
o: Power cables, the PDU outlet and its breaker
Right. No lights at all points to no power reaching it.
The RAID array's consistency check from the controller BIOS
No power means nothing to check yet.
The OS boot loader
The server isn't getting power, let alone booting.
The DNS record for the server
DNS doesn't affect power.

q.q: A RAID 5 array was degraded. During the rebuild, a second drive failed. What's the result?
o: The hot spare rebuilds both missing drives one after the other
A spare replaces one drive; two failures already broke RAID 5.
The controller turns it into RAID 0
Controllers don't switch RAID levels to save data.
The array keeps running on parity
Parity covers one missing drive, not two.
The array fails and data must be restored from backup
Right. RAID 5 survives only one drive failure.

q.q: After a controller battery failed, writes to an array got much slower. Reads are normal. What happened?
o: The filesystem ran out of inodes
That stops new files; it doesn't slow writes.
The server lost its DNS record
DNS doesn't affect local disk writes.
The controller switched from write-back to write-through cache
Right. Without battery protection, the controller turns off write caching to stay safe.
The array lost a drive and is now running in degraded mode on parity
A degraded array usually slows reads too.

q.q: A Linux server says No space left on device, but df -h shows 40% free. What should you check?
o: RAM use with free -m
Memory isn't disk space.
The CPU load with uptime
CPU load doesn't cause this error.
Network routes with ip route
Routes don't affect local disk.
Inode use with df -i
Right. Millions of tiny files can use all inodes while blocks stay free.

q.q: After a disk was replaced, a Linux server stops at boot waiting for a data volume. The disk works. What's the likely cause?
o: /etc/fstab refers to the old disk's UUID
Right. A new disk has a new UUID, so the old fstab entry no longer matches.
The root password expired
That wouldn't stop the boot mount.
The NIC driver is missing
That causes network trouble, not mount failures.
The server's DNS server address is set wrong
Local mounts don't use DNS.

q.q: After a new drive is added, a server says Operating system not found. The old boot drive is fine. What's the likely cause?
o: The new drive wiped the old one
Adding a drive doesn't erase another.
The OS license expired
Licensing doesn't block finding the boot drive.
The boot order now points to the new drive
Right. Firmware may try the new drive first; set the boot order back.
The PSU is too weak
A weak PSU causes power problems, not this error.

q.q: /var on a Linux server fills up every few days. Which command finds what's using the space?
o: du -sh /var/* | sort -h
Right. du totals each folder's size; sorting shows the biggest.
ip addr
That shows network addresses.
free -h
That shows memory.
df -i /var
That shows inodes, not which folders are large.

q.q: A backup service fails to start after the account it runs as got a new password. What fixes it?
o: Reinstall the operating system from the original installation media
Far more than needed.
Restart the domain controller so the new password replicates to it
The password change already took effect.
Update the service's saved credentials with the new password
Right. The service still has the old password stored.
Delete the service account
The service would have no account to run as.

q.q: An application's memory use grows steadily for days until the server slows, then drops back after a reboot. What's the likely cause?
o: A DNS cache that's too small
DNS cache size doesn't cause growing memory use.
A memory leak in the application
Right. Memory that's never released grows until restart.
A failed power supply
That doesn't follow a slow climb that resets on reboot.
A full disk on the data volume
Disk space and memory use are different.

q.q: A Windows server crashes with a stop error right after a storage driver update. What should you try first?
o: Replace the system board
The hardware worked fine before the update.
Increase the page file size
Page file size doesn't fix a bad driver.
Reformat the data volumes
That loses data and doesn't fix the driver.
Boot to safe mode and roll back the driver
Right. The new driver is the change, so undo it.

q.q: A systemd service named reports fails to start on a Linux server. Which command shows its recent log messages?
o: chmod -R 755 reports
That changes permissions; it doesn't show logs.
journalctl -u reports
Right. journalctl -u shows the journal entries for one unit.
ip route
That shows the routing table.
df -h
That shows disk space.

q.q: After last night's patch, an app on a server crashes on start. Other servers without the patch are fine. What should you do?
o: Reinstall the app with its default settings and import the old data afterward
That may lose its configuration and doesn't address the patch.
Turn off automatic updates forever
That leaves servers unpatched.
Roll back the patch as the change plan allows and report it to the vendor
Right. The patch is the most likely cause, so undo it and tell the vendor.
Patch every other server too so they match
That would break them too.

q.q: Users can't log on to a member server. The event log shows Kerberos errors, and the server's clock is 15 minutes behind. What should you fix?
o: The DHCP scope size and lease length for the server's subnet
DHCP doesn't set the clock.
The server's RAID level
Storage doesn't affect logon.
The server's time sync with the domain time source
Right. Kerberos fails when clocks differ by more than 5 minutes.
The users' passwords
Their passwords work on other servers.

q.q: A server shows IPv4 address 169.254.18.40. What does that tell you?
o: It has a valid public address
169.254 is link-local, not public.
It couldn't reach a DHCP server and assigned itself an APIPA address
Right. 169.254.x.x is self-assigned when DHCP fails.
DNS gave it a temporary address
DNS resolves names; it doesn't hand out addresses.
It's configured with a static address from the reserved private range
APIPA is automatic.

q.q: A server can ping 10.1.1.20 but not fileserv.base.example. Which tool checks the likely cause?
o: netstat -r
Routing works because the IP ping succeeds.
arp -a
ARP maps IPs to MACs; IP connectivity already works.
nslookup
Right. IP works but the name doesn't, which points to DNS.
ipconfig /release
That drops the IP address and makes it worse.

q.q: A server can reach every host on its own subnet but nothing on any other subnet. What's the most likely cause?
o: A wrong DNS server address in its settings
That affects names, not IP reachability.
A bad Ethernet cable
Then local hosts wouldn't work either.
A full disk
Disks don't affect routing.
A wrong or missing default gateway
Right. Traffic to other subnets goes through the gateway.

q.q: A server loses its connection every few minutes, and the log shows a duplicate IP address. What's happening?
o: Another device is using the same IP address
Right. Two devices with one IP fight over ARP, so traffic goes to whichever answered last.
The NIC is in a team
Teaming is supported and doesn't cause conflicts.
The switch port is a trunk
Trunking doesn't cause address conflicts.
The server's DNS record has a typo in its hostname
DNS wouldn't cause duplicate address warnings.

q.q: A server was moved to a new switch port. The link light is on, the IP is static and correct, but it can't reach anything. What should you check?
o: The VLAN assigned to the new switch port
Right. A port in the wrong VLAN puts the server on the wrong network.
The server's CPU usage
CPU use doesn't block connectivity.
The NTP server address in the time settings
Time doesn't block network reachability.
The server's RAID controller
Storage isn't involved.

q.q: Ping to a web server works, but browsers can't connect on port 443. What's the likely cause?
o: A wrong default gateway
Ping works, so routing is fine.
A wrong subnet mask
Ping already reaches it.
A failed NIC
A dead NIC wouldn't answer pings.
A firewall blocking TCP 443
Right. ICMP gets through but the HTTPS port is blocked.

q.q: A user was just added to the group that has access to a share, but still gets Access denied. What's the quickest fix?
o: Grant the user full control directly
That bypasses group-based access.
Have the user log off and back on to refresh group membership
Right. Group membership is read at logon into the access token.
Reset the share's NTFS permissions so inheritance applies again
The permissions are already correct.
Reinstall the file server role
The role works; the token is old.

q.q: A share grants Everyone Read. The NTFS permission on the folder grants the user Modify. What can the user do over the network?
o: Modify
The share permission limits it to Read.
Nothing at all
Both allow at least Read.
Read only
Right. Over the network, the most restrictive of share and NTFS permissions wins.
Full control
Neither permission grants Full Control.

q.q: Users get browser warnings when they open an internal web app that worked yesterday. The warning says the certificate isn't valid. What's the likely cause?
o: The server's certificate expired
Right. Expired certificates trigger warnings until renewed.
The server's RAID array is degraded
Storage doesn't affect certificates.
The DNS cache is full
DNS cache size doesn't cause certificate errors.
The users' passwords expired
That would block logons, not show certificate warnings.

q.q: A server shows an unknown process making outbound connections at 3 AM to an outside address. What should you do first?
o: Ignore it, since it only runs outside working hours when nobody is affected
Off-hours activity is a common sign of compromise.
Delete the process's file and keep using the server
That destroys evidence and may not remove the threat.
Isolate the server from the network and start incident response
Right. Contain it first so possible malware can't spread or send out more data.
Reboot the server to clear the process
Rebooting can destroy evidence and the malware may come back.

q.q: The server's security log shows hundreds of failed logons a minute for different usernames from one IP. What is this?
o: A DNS misconfiguration
DNS errors don't make failed logons.
A password-spraying or brute-force attack
Right. Many failed logons from one source is an attack on credentials.
A failing hard drive
Hardware faults don't create logon attempts.
A normal user who forgot their password
One user wouldn't try hundreds of different usernames.

q.q: A port scan finds TCP 23 open on a production server. What should you do?
o: Open TCP 22 next to it
Telnet would still be open.
Disable Telnet and use SSH for remote admin
Right. Telnet sends everything, including passwords, in clear text.
Move Telnet to port 2323
Hiding it on another port isn't security.
Leave it open but change the Telnet banner
A new banner doesn't add encryption.

q.title: Place the storage for a three-host virtual cluster
q.scenario: Three hypervisor hosts run the unit's virtual machines (VMs). Match each storage need to the right storage design. Three items in the tray do not fit any need here.
q.ticket: Change CHG-3318. Each host has 2 small drive bays. The database server has free drive bays and runs many small writes. Policy: no RAID 0 for data.

slots.label: Office file shares
slots.hint: reached from user PCs on the office LAN

devs.name: RAID 1 (2 SSDs)
devs.why: A mirror keeps a full copy on the second drive, so a host still boots after one drive fails. It needs only the 2 bays each host has.

devs.name: iSCSI SAN LUN
devs.why: A SAN hands out block storage over the storage network. A LUN (a logical disk) can be shared by all hosts, which failover clustering needs so a VM can restart on another host, which clustered VM features need for moving VMs between hosts.

devs.name: NAS with SMB shares
devs.why: A NAS shares files over the LAN by name. Users map it as a network drive, which is what a file share needs.

devs.name: RAID 10 (4 SSDs)
devs.why: RAID 10 mirrors and stripes, so it writes fast with no parity math and survives a drive loss. That suits many small writes.

devs.name: RAID 0 (2 drives)
devs.why: RAID 0 stripes with no redundancy. One failed drive loses everything, so it must not hold data the unit cannot lose.

devs.name: RAID 5 (4 SSDs)
devs.why: RAID 5 survives one drive loss but every small write costs extra parity reads and writes. It is a weak fit for a write-heavy database.

devs.name: RAID 6 (4 SSDs)
devs.why: RAID 6 survives two drive losses but writes two sets of parity, so small writes are slower still. It fits capacity and safety more than write speed.

q.title: Patch a two-node cluster with little downtime
q.scenario: FS-CL1 is a two-node Windows failover cluster. FS01 is active and runs the file-share role. FS02 is the passive standby. Put the steps in order so every node gets this month's patches and users lose as little access as possible. Some listed steps do not belong.
q.ticket: CHG-4410: monthly patching window. Both nodes are Up. Patches need a restart to finish.

rules.text: Confirm both nodes are Up and a recent backup exists
rules.why: Check health and have a way back before you change anything. A cluster that is already unhealthy can lose its role when a node restarts.

rules.text: Patch and restart FS02 (the passive node)
rules.why: The passive node serves no users, so patching it first causes no outage.

rules.text: Check FS02 is Up and rejoined the cluster
rules.why: You must know FS02 came back healthy before you move the role onto it.

rules.text: Move the file role to FS02 (planned failover)
rules.why: A planned move shifts the role in a short pause. FS01 is then idle and safe to patch.
FS01 now serves no users, so its restart does not hit them.

rules.text: Confirm both nodes are Up and the role is Online
rules.why: The final check proves the cluster is whole and the shares work again. Nothing should come after it.

rules.text: Patch and restart both nodes at the same time
rules.why: Both nodes would be down together and the shares would be offline. Patching one node at a time is the point of a cluster.

rules.text: Patch and restart FS01 (the active node) first
rules.why: Restarting the node that holds the role drops the file shares for everyone. Patch the passive node first and move the role in a short pause.

rules.text: Evict FS02 from the cluster, then patch it
rules.why: Evicting removes the node from the cluster setup, and it has to be added back later. Normal patching never needs it.

before.why: Check health and the backup before the first change.
You can only check the result after the patch and restart finish.
Never move the role onto a node you have not verified.
FS01 must give up the role before it restarts, or users lose access when it restarts.

last.why: A final check only has value when all the work is done.

checks.t: Read the array state (mdstat or mdadm --detail)
checks.why: /proc/mdstat shows [3/2] [U_U], which means 2 of 3 members are working and one slot is empty. mdadm --detail says the same as 'clean, degraded'. Start by reading the facts.

checks.t: Find which disk is the blank new one
checks.why: lsblk lists every disk and what is on it. sde has no partitions and no mount point, so it is the new disk. sdf holds the mounted /srv/backup, so it is not free.

checks.t: Check the two surviving disks' health
checks.why: A rebuild reads every sector of the surviving disks. If one of them is also failing, a second failure during the rebuild would lose the array, so check them first (smartctl).

checks.t: Add the new disk /dev/sde to md0
checks.why: mdadm --add puts the blank disk in as the missing member and starts the rebuild. The array stays online while it rebuilds.
After the add, /proc/mdstat shows a recovery line and mdadm --detail shows 'recovering'. Always confirm the rebuild is running and watch for errors.

checks.t: Did not add a disk that is in use
checks.why: sdf holds the mounted /srv/backup and sda is the OS disk. Adding either to the array would overwrite its data if it were allowed.
mdadm --create writes new metadata over the disks. It can destroy the data on a RAID that only needs a replacement disk. A degraded array is repaired with --add, not rebuilt from scratch.

q.title: Read the backup server log after a missed weekend
q.scenario: You take over the backup duty on Tuesday morning. The file server FS01 should get an incremental backup every night. Read the log from bk01, mark every line that points to a backup problem, then say what it means for the data.
q.ticket: Ticket 7731: the commander wants to know how far back FS01's data would be lost if its disks failed today.

lines.text: Nov 20 01:00:02 bk01 backupd[811]: job FS01-inc started (incremental, day 3 of 7-day chain)
lines.why: A normal start of the nightly incremental job (it saves only what changed since the last run).

lines.text: Nov 20 01:14:37 bk01 backupd[811]: job FS01-inc finished: 18.4 GB written, 0 warnings, restore point RP-0120 created
lines.why: A healthy run. A restore point is a saved copy you can recover from, and this one was created with no warnings.

lines.text: Nov 21 01:00:04 bk01 backupd[811]: job FS01-inc started (incremental, day 4 of 7-day chain)
lines.why: A normal start of the next night's job.

lines.text: Nov 21 01:09:55 bk01 backupd[811]: repository /mnt/repo: 96% full, 31 GB free, retention keeps 14 chains
lines.why: The storage that holds the backups was almost full. This early warning explains the failures that follow.

lines.text: Nov 21 01:13:50 bk01 backupd[811]: job FS01-inc finished: 18.1 GB written, 0 warnings, restore point RP-0121 created
lines.why: The last good run in this log. RP-0121 is the newest restore point that exists.

lines.text: Nov 22 01:00:03 bk01 backupd[811]: job FS01-inc started (incremental, day 5 of 7-day chain)
lines.why: A normal start. The problem shows up later in the run.

lines.text: Nov 22 01:03:41 bk01 backupd[811]: write failed on /mnt/repo/FS01/FS01-inc-0122.vib: No space left on device
lines.why: The backup could not write because the repository is full.

lines.text: Nov 22 01:03:42 bk01 backupd[811]: job FS01-inc FAILED, no restore point created
lines.why: The job failed, so there is no copy of the data from this night.

lines.text: Nov 23 01:00:09 bk01 backupd[811]: job FS01-inc FAILED: cannot create chain file: No space left on device
lines.why: The same failure again the next night. Backups have now failed two nights in a row.

lines.text: Nov 23 06:30:00 bk01 backupd[811]: verify RP-0121 checksum OK
lines.why: A scheduled check shows the Nov 21 restore point is intact. Good news, but it is also the newest valid copy.

lines.text: Nov 24 01:00:08 bk01 backupd[811]: job FS01-inc FAILED: cannot create chain file: No space left on device
lines.why: A third failed night in a row, so changes made since Nov 21 are not protected.

lines.text: Nov 24 07:45:12 bk01 mailer[640]: report mailed to backup-ops@unit.example
lines.why: Just the daily report mail. It does not show a problem by itself.

ask.label: If FS01's disks failed this morning, how far back would data be lost?
opts: To RP-0121 on Nov 21, about 3 days, because the backup account password expired
To RP-0120 on Nov 20, about 4 days, because RP-0121 is corrupt
To RP-0121 on Nov 21, about 3 days, because the repository is full
To RP-0121 on Nov 21, about 3 days, because the nightly job was disabled
ask.why: RP-0121 from Nov 21 is the newest restore point. Every job since Nov 22 failed with 'No space left on device' after the repository reached 96% full. The Nov 23 check of RP-0121 passed, so it is not corrupt. The jobs ran and failed, so they were not disabled, and no login error appears, so it is not a password problem.

q.title: Read the management controller log of a server that shut off
q.scenario: Server DB05 turned itself off overnight and the database was down until morning. The base's monitoring tool missed it. You pulled the System Event Log (SEL) from the server's management controller (BMC). Mark every line that is part of the failure, then say what happened.
q.ticket: INC-6141: DB05 down 03:21 to 07:58. The BMC SEL is below (ipmitool sel elist style).

lines.text: 12 | 11/24/2026 | 22:00:14 | Power Supply PS2 Status | Power Supply AC lost | Asserted
lines.why: PS2 lost its AC input for a moment. The next line shows it came back, and the log shows no shutdown at this time. It is a side event, not the cause.

lines.text: 13 | 11/24/2026 | 22:00:41 | Power Supply PS2 Status | Power Supply AC lost | Deasserted
lines.why: Deasserted means the condition cleared. PS2 has AC power again after 27 seconds.

lines.text: 14 | 11/24/2026 | 22:40:02 | Fan Fan3 | Lower Critical going low  | Asserted | Reading 0 < Threshold 1500 RPM
lines.why: Fan 3 reads 0 RPM, which means it has stopped. This is where the trouble starts.

lines.text: 15 | 11/24/2026 | 22:40:05 | Fan Fan Redundancy | Redundancy Lost | Asserted
lines.why: The server lost its spare cooling capacity because one fan is dead. It still runs, but with no margin.

lines.text: 16 | 11/25/2026 | 01:15:30 | Session Audit BMC | Session Activated | Asserted | User ID 2, Web
lines.why: Someone logged in to the BMC web page. An admin login by itself is normal.

lines.text: 17 | 11/25/2026 | 03:05:48 | Temperature CPU1 Temp | Upper Non-critical going high | Asserted | Reading 83 > Threshold 80 degrees C
lines.why: The CPU is above its warning temperature. Heat is building without the working fan.

lines.text: 18 | 11/25/2026 | 03:21:09 | Temperature CPU1 Temp | Upper Critical going high | Asserted | Reading 96 > Threshold 95 degrees C
lines.why: The CPU passed its critical limit. The next step is a protective shutdown.

lines.text: 19 | 11/25/2026 | 03:21:11 | Processor CPU1 Status | Thermal Trip | Asserted
lines.why: A thermal trip is the CPU shutting the server off to protect itself from heat damage. This is the moment of the outage.

lines.text: 20 | 11/25/2026 | 07:58:40 | System Boot Initiated | Initiated by power up | Asserted
lines.why: The server was powered back on in the morning. A normal event.

lines.text: 21 | 11/25/2026 | 07:58:52 | Power Supply PS1 Status | Presence detected | Asserted
lines.why: The power supply is simply detected at boot. It reports no fault.

lines.text: 22 | 11/25/2026 | 07:59:30 | Drive Slot Bay 2 | Drive Present | Asserted
lines.why: A drive is detected in its bay at boot. No fault is reported.

ask.label: What most likely happened?
opts: A power supply lost AC input briefly, so the server lost power
A fan failed, the CPU overheated and tripped its heat shutdown
A failed drive crashed the operating system, then it restarted
An admin shut the server down from the BMC web page
ask.why: The fan stopped first, then the CPU temperature rose past warning and critical limits, and a thermal trip followed. PS2's AC loss cleared 27 seconds later at 22:00 and was hours before the shutdown. No drive fault appears, and the admin login came about two hours before the trip with no power command logged.

checks.why: ipconfig or Get-NetIPConfiguration shows the address, mask, gateway and DNS in one place. The default gateway is 10.20.30.254.
The default route is where the server sends any traffic for another subnet. Here it points to 10.20.30.254, which is not the VLAN's gateway.
A reply from 10.20.30.1 proves the link and subnet work and the real gateway is alive. That narrows the fault to the gateway setting on APP07.

Traffic for other subnets goes to the default gateway. The configured address has no device behind it, so the traffic never leaves. Setting the gateway to 10.20.30.1 replaces it. Adding a second default route alone does not remove the bad one.
